claims.text: The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
The baseline alloy has limited strain hardening and poor uniform deformability and fails rapidly at high strain rate.
Cold deformation followed by controlled dual annealing can produce a bimodal distribution of submicron grains in a coarser-grained matrix.
Fine grains strengthen the alloy by impeding dislocation motion.
Fine grains delay incipient shear-band formation.
Coarse grains preserve ductility by accommodating plastic strain.
Ultrafine-grained regions increase dynamic strain hardening by increasing obstacles to dislocation glide and promoting dislocation storage.
Coarse-grained regions facilitate uniform plastic flow.
Combining ultrafine and coarse grains reduces abrupt strain localization and rapid failure during adiabatic high-strain-rate deformation.
The bimodal microstructure will increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to the baseline.
The bimodal microstructure will increase compressive strength relative to the baseline.
The bimodal microstructure will increase fracture strain from 13.5% toward 18–20%.
The bimodal microstructure will improve resistance to shear localization.
The bimodal microstructure will increase dynamically absorbed impact energy.
The predicted improvements apply under adiabatic dynamic loading at strain rates of approximately 10^3–10^4 s^-1.
The predicted improvements may not extend to low-strain-rate or thermally equilibrated loading.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and measurements predict increased absorbed impact energy, but the predicted-outcome field calls this increased 'impact-induced energy release.' Energy absorption and energy release are not equivalent outcomes, and increased absorption cannot by itself demonstrate increased release.
